title: Acute psychosis: A neuropsychiatric dilemma
case_prompt: A 68-year-old man was brought with a 1-day history of acute severe agitation, extreme fearfulness on seeing his reflection, and refusal of food and water, preceded by 5 days of untreated low-grade fever and headache. Six months earlier he had an unprovoked stray dog bite (Class I) with no post-exposure antirabies vaccination. His hypertension was treated irregularly; there was no history of head injury, other medical or psychiatric illness, or substance use. On examination, he was afebrile, alert, and oriented; pulse 110/min, blood pressure 160/110 mm Hg. Plantar responses were bilaterally extensor and optic fundi were normal. Mental status examination showed increased psychomotor activity, ideas of reference, and visual hallucinations; primary cognition was intact, but judgment and insight were impaired. Biochemical tests, chest radiograph, electrocardiogram, and electroencephalogram were normal. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed multiple vascular infarcts and demyelinating patches secondary to vascular, toxic, or inflammatory etiologies, suggesting multiple vascular infarcts in different stages of evolution or rabies encephalitis. A contrast-enhanced MRI after 48 hours showed the same findings.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Rabies encephalitis was initially considered due to the history of dog bite without prophylaxis but excluded because of rapid clinical improvement — “With a history of Class 1 dog bite and no post exposure prophylaxis our first consideration for differential diagnosis was rabies...However the patient's improvement so early in the intervention ruled out the diagnosis of rabies.”  
2. HSV encephalitis was considered given the preceding fever, headache, and MRI demyelinating patches but could not be confirmed without CSF analysis — “We also considered HSV encephalitis as patient presented with h/o fever and headache and altered behavior...The definitive diagnosis requires cerebrospinal fluid studies…unfortunately…lumbar puncture was not done.”  
3. Cerebrovascular accident was considered based on his hypertension, headache, and the presence of multiple infarcts on MRI, and became most likely when contrast MRI showed vascular lesions — “When brain MRI with contrast was done, the diagnosis of CVA looked more likely.”
